# Adversarial implementation review — 12 September 2026

The reviewed origin revision is `a162fb909d45b8bcdb54f1939f2230f0419423c1`.
The review covered all three Workers, shared packages, unit and integration tests,
CI workflows, dependency configuration, and the service/deployment contracts.
Three collaborators independently examined ingress, processing/token exchange,
and tooling; the implementation was then checked against the combined findings.
The original checkout and its untracked research files were preserved in place.

The main problem was failure handling: a green baseline did not prove that a
reaction had been created, that an unreadable error was permanent, or that a
validated job could form its promised URL. The existing package and Worker
interfaces are small and useful. Broad restructuring would add churn without
resolving these defects.

## Implemented findings

### P2: Redirects could acknowledge a reaction that never happened

At origin, `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor/src/github/reactions.ts`
used default Fetch redirect handling and accepted any final `200` or `201`.
A Workerd reproduction showed a `301` transforming the reaction POST into a
GET with no body; a `200` reaction-list response then looked like successful
creation. This matters when a repository URL redirects after a rename or move.

The processor now repeats the original POST for `301`, `302`, `307`, and `308`,
up to three redirects, only within `https://api.github.com` and without URL
credentials. It retains the same token and body. Intermediate body cancellation
does not delay the request. Unsafe, unsupported, or exhausted redirects follow
the existing permanent-failure path. A real Worker integration fixture requires
the redirected request to retain the exact method, credentials, and body.

This follows GitHub's instruction to [repeat redirected requests](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#follow-redirects),
accounts for [Fetch's POST-to-GET behavior](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-redirect-fetch),
and avoids Cloudflare's [cross-host forwarding of authorization headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/request/#properties).

### P2: Incomplete `403` diagnostics could discard retryable jobs

The processor used error-body text to recognize secondary rate limits. It retried
a timed-out `403` read, but acknowledged an errored or oversized read even though
both also prevented classification. Existing tests explicitly expected that loss.

Stream exceptions and the 16 KiB cutoff now produce `bodyReadFailed: true` and
retry `403` responses. Header diagnostics and retry hints survive. Fully received
empty or malformed bodies keep the status/header policy; other statuses keep
their existing behavior. The one-second diagnostic deadline and best-effort
cancellation remain intact. This policy applies GitHub's [rate-limit guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#handle-rate-limit-errors-appropriately)
without treating a failed diagnostic read as proof of permanent denial.

### P2: The broker client rejected valid OAuth response variants

`packages/token-exchange/src/index.ts` required exactly `Bearer` and an explicit
response `scope`. OAuth token types are case-insensitive, and an unchanged scope
may be omitted. Valid responses therefore threw and caused unnecessary retries.

The client accepts case variations of `Bearer` and uses the validated requested
scope only when response scope is absent. Explicit scope values remain authoritative;
null, empty, and non-string scopes remain invalid. The installation-token profile
still requires its existing expiration and issued-token-type fields. Literal
response regressions failed four times before the fix and pass afterward.
See [RFC 8693 §2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1)
and [RFC 6749 §5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749.html#section-5.1).

### P2: Accepted jobs could fail or change meaning during URL construction

`packages/github-webhook-jobs/src/index.ts` accepted `.` and `..` repository parts,
which URL parsing normalizes, and lone surrogates, which `encodeURIComponent`
rejects. Signed deliveries could publish jobs that did not preserve the intended
repository resource or failed before reaching the broker.

The shared parser now rejects these values before publication and consumption.
Tests preserve ordinary dotted names, percent literals, and well-formed Unicode.
This is a canonical-resource correctness fix, not a demonstrated authentication
bypass: queue writers and signed webhook bodies remain within the documented trust
model. See the [URL dot-segment rules](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#single-dot-url-path-segment)
and [ECMAScript URI encoding](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/global-object.html#sec-encodeuricomponent-uricomponent).

### P3: Invalid UTF-8 was silently repaired before JSON parsing

The receiver authenticated exact bytes but decoded them with replacement before
parsing JSON. Signed malformed UTF-8 could therefore receive `202` despite the
valid-JSON contract. Fatal UTF-8 decoding now shares the authenticated JSON error
path and returns `400`. Bad signatures still return `401` before decoding.
Tests cover invalid bytes, overlong/truncated encodings, and valid non-ASCII text.
See [RFC 8259 §8.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-8.1)
and [TextDecoder error handling](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-textdecoder).

### P3: Secret retrieval failures escaped the receiver's response contract

A rejecting Secrets Store `get()` escaped the receiver handler instead of producing
its documented configuration error. The receiver now returns `500` problem details
with a fixed diagnostic event, excluding the exception's text, and publishes no
job. The regression includes a secret-like failure message and checks the exact safe
log. The asynchronous binding is described in [Cloudflare's Secrets Store integration](https://developers.cloudflare.com/secrets-store/integrations/workers/#3-access-the-secret-on-the-env-object).

### P3: Expired dependency exceptions and contradictory README text

Ten version-specific cooldown exceptions had expired on 10 September. An isolated
archive without them passed `pnpm up -r --lockfile-only --ignore-scripts`,
`pnpm dedupe --lockfile-only --ignore-scripts`, and a frozen install. The exceptions
were removed; dependency versions and the source lockfile were preserved.
See [pnpm's release-age exclusions](https://pnpm.io/10.x/settings#minimumreleaseageexclude).

The README incorrectly said that all non-ping events created no job. It now states
that newly created status comments create jobs. The service and implementation
documents describe each changed behavior.

## Simplification decisions

- Exact job-key validation now checks the enumerable key set directly, removing
  two sorts and a copied array. It retains the rejection of unexpected fields,
  including the adversarial non-enumerable-property case.
- The redirect policy stays private to reaction creation. A generic HTTP client,
  configurable retry framework, or extra dependency interface would increase the
  public surface for one operation.
- The HTTP, job-contract, and token-exchange packages retain their existing
  interfaces. Flattening them would spread shared validation or broker knowledge
  across Workers and tests.
- The queue and GitHub's existing-reaction success semantics already address
  repeated delivery. An additional deduplication database is not justified by
  the current operation.
- Repository/author authorization, the permission pair, separate deployment
  ownership, and separate CI workflows are explicit project choices. No evidence
  justified silently replacing them during this review.

## Remaining concerns and verification limits

The source deployment-dispatch workflow does not pass the successful source SHA;
the deployment updater follows the latest source branch. A successful revision A
can therefore trigger a proposal containing newer revision B. The deployment
repository checks the proposed source, so this is not an unchecked-deployment
bypass. Exact revision propagation needs a coordinated change in both repositories;
only this project's implementation was changed here.

Issuer RPC, broker response reading, and the initial GitHub fetch have no explicit
application deadline. The existing byte limits do not bound elapsed time. This is
a remaining resilience design question: choose budgets from dependency latency and
queue-processing requirements, then test cancellation and error classification
together. No production latency or outage was measured in this review.

Local fixtures validate the issuer/broker interfaces and actual Worker execution;
they do not validate production broker policy, live GitHub App permissions,
production routes, queue provisioning, or Secrets Store permissions. No production
deployment or live GitHub mutation was performed.

## Validation and final review

Baseline: `node --run check` passed all gates and 153 tests at the pinned origin.
New regressions were first demonstrated against the original implementation.
Final validation and the independent Standards and Spec review results are recorded
when the complete patch has passed the repository gates.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/processor_review
Payload:
Implemented and verified two processor fixes:

- **Redirect data loss:** Workerd reproduced `POST → 301 → GET → 200`, falsely completing a reaction job. The processor now preserves POST/body/authorization across at most three permitted GitHub redirects and rejects unsafe destinations.
- **Lost retries:** Unreadable or oversized `403` bodies now trigger retries with bounded header diagnostics.

All **53 processor tests passed**, including a real Workerd redirect regression; test typechecking passed. Existing nonblocking response cancellation behavior remains covered.

Choices follow [GitHub redirect guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#follow-redirects), [reaction endpoint semantics](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reactions/reactions#create-reaction-for-an-issue-comment), and [Cloudflare’s credential-forwarding warning](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/request/#properties).

No further confirmed processor defect found. Live GitHub/broker behavior was not exercised. Missing application deadlines remain a pre-existing resilience consideration.

- Job validation, authenticated fatal UTF-8 decoding, safe secret-resolution failure handling, and key-validation simplification match the specified contracts.

name: code-review
description: "Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \"review since X\"."
---

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name**: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code**: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps**: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession**: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches**: the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery**: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change**: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality**: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains**: long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man**: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest**: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.
# Contributing

Keep changes small, explicit, and grounded in the service contract.

Before opening a pull request:

1. Run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
2. Run `node --run check`.
3. Update `docs/service-contract.md` when externally observable behaviour changes.
4. Update `docs/implementation.md` when package layout, Worker entrypoints, request flow, or bindings change.
5. Update `docs/deployment.md` and `docs/release.md` when source/deployment ownership or publish-readiness checks change.
6. Update `CONTEXT.md` when terminology or trust-boundary language changes.

Do not commit local deployment state or secrets. In particular, keep `.dev.vars`, `.env`, `.wrangler/`, `.local-secrets/`, Cloudflare tokens, and webhook secrets out of commits.

Use present-tense documentation for implemented behaviour.
# cyspbot documentation

- [Service contract](service-contract.md) is authoritative for the webhook receiver's observable HTTP behavior.
- [Implementation](implementation.md) describes the workspace packages, Worker entrypoint, bindings, and validation commands.
- [Deployment](deployment.md) describes the public-source and production-deployment boundaries.
- [Release checklist](release.md) covers source and documentation verification.

{"baseRefOid":"a162fb909d45b8bcdb54f1939f2230f0419423c1","body":"GitHub redirects could turn a reaction POST into a GET whose `200` response incorrectly completed the queue job. Preserve the POST, body, and authorization across up to three supported redirects within `https://api.github.com`, and retry `403` responses when incomplete diagnostics prevent rate-limit classification.

Also accept case-insensitive OAuth Bearer responses and omitted unchanged scopes; reject repository parts that cannot preserve their URL segment; reject authenticated malformed UTF-8; and return safe problem details when secret retrieval fails. Simplify exact job-key validation, remove expired dependency cooldown exceptions after isolated resolution probes, and update the service contract.

Validation:

- `node --run check`: 195 tests pass, plus formatting, generated types, lint, TypeScript, Knip, and all three Worker deploy dry runs.
- `node --run test:coverage`: 99.69% statements, 98.51% branches, 100% lines.
- Regression failures reproduced before the fixes, including a real Workerd redirect test.
- Independent Standards and Spec reviews found no remaining source findings.

name: code-review
description: "Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \"review since X\"."
---

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name**: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code**: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps**: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession**: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches**: the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery**: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change**: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality**: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains**: long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man**: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest**: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.
# Contributing

Keep changes small, explicit, and grounded in the service contract.

Before opening a pull request:

1. Run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
2. Run `node --run check`.
3. Update `docs/service-contract.md` when externally observable behaviour changes.
4. Update `docs/implementation.md` when package layout, Worker entrypoints, request flow, or bindings change.
5. Update `docs/deployment.md` and `docs/release.md` when source/deployment ownership or publish-readiness checks change.
6. Update `CONTEXT.md` when terminology or trust-boundary language changes.

Do not commit local deployment state or secrets. In particular, keep `.dev.vars`, `.env`, `.wrangler/`, `.local-secrets/`, Cloudflare tokens, and webhook secrets out of commits.

Use present-tense documentation for implemented behaviour.
# cyspbot documentation

- [Service contract](service-contract.md) is authoritative for the webhook receiver's observable HTTP behavior.
- [Implementation](implementation.md) describes the workspace packages, Worker entrypoint, bindings, and validation commands.
- [Deployment](deployment.md) describes the public-source and production-deployment boundaries.
- [Release checklist](release.md) covers source and documentation verification.

L11: # Pull requests
L12: 
L13: Propose, review, and merge code changes using pull requests to collaborate effectively and maintain code quality.
L14: 
L15: Copy as Markdown
L16: ## In this article
L17: 
L18:   * cite4†Working with pull requests L19:   * cite5†Draft pull requests L20:   * cite6†Pull request refs and merge branches L21:   * cite7†Differences between commits on compare and pull request pages L22:   * cite8†Collaborative development models L23:   * cite9†Further reading L24: Pull requests are proposals to merge code changes into a project. A pull request is GitHub's key collaboration feature, letting you discuss and review changes before merging them. This helps teams work together, catch issues early, and maintain code quality.
L25: 
L26: cite10†View your pull requests†github.com L27: ## cite4†Working with pull requests L28: 
L29: A pull request brings together the context reviewers need to understand a change. This context is organized into tabs:
L30:   * The Conversation tab shows the description, timeline, comments, and reviews.
L31:   * The Commits tab shows how the pull request branch changed over time.
L32:   * The Checks tab shows automated tests, builds, and other validations.
L33:   * The Files changed tab shows the diff that reviewers use to understand the proposed changes.
L34:   * The Findings tab shows automated code review results, such as code scanning alerts, for the proposed changes.
L35: Separately from the tabs, the merge status highlights blockers, missing approvals, and other requirements before merging. It appears in the pull request header and in the merge box.
L36: 
L37: Together, these views help authors and reviewers discuss the change, track feedback, and decide when the pull request is ready to merge.
L38: ## cite5†Draft pull requests L39: 
L40: When you create a pull request, you can choose to make it a draft pull request. Draft pull requests cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically requested to review them. Drafts are useful when you want to share work-in-progress without formally requesting reviews.
L41: When you're ready to get feedback on your pull request, you can mark your draft pull request as ready for review. Marking a pull request as ready for review will request reviews from any code owners. You can convert a pull request to a draft at any time. See cite11†Changing the stage of a pull request .
L42: ## cite6†Pull request refs and merge branches L43: 
L44: When you open a pull request, GitHub creates temporary Git references that point to the pull request's head branch and, when possible, to a simulated merge result. These refs help GitHub and integrations evaluate the pull request without changing the base branch.
L45: For most contributors, these refs stay in the background. They are most relevant when you are building automation, debugging CI behavior, or fetching pull request state locally. For information about how GitHub Actions uses the merge branch, see cite12†Events that trigger workflows .
L46: ## cite7†Differences between commits on compare and pull request pages L47: 
L48: Compare pages and pull request pages can calculate changed files from different merge bases. As a result, the same branches can sometimes show different diffs in each place.
L49: 
L50: This usually matters when the base branch has changed since the pull request was created. Pull request pages focus on what the pull request introduced, while compare pages reflect the current comparison between two refs.
L51: ## cite8†Collaborative development models L52: 
L53: The way you use pull requests depends on the type of development model you use in your project. You can use the fork and pull model or the shared repository model.
L54: ### cite13†Fork and pull model L55: 
L56: In the fork and pull model, anyone can fork an existing ("upstream") repository if they have read access and the owner of the upstream repository allows it. Be aware that a fork and its upstream share the same Git data. This means that all content uploaded to a fork is accessible from the upstream and all other forks of that upstream.
L57: You do not need permission from the upstream repository to push to a fork you created. You can optionally allow anyone with push access to the upstream repository to make changes to your pull request branch. This model is popular with open-source projects because it reduces friction for new contributors and lets people work independently without upfront coordination.
L58: 
L59: Tip
L60: For more information on open source, specifically how to create and grow an open source project, we've created cite14†Open Source Guides†opensource.guide that will help you foster a healthy open source community. You can also take a free cite15†GitHub Skills†skills.github.com course on maintaining open source communities.
L61: ### cite16†Shared repository model L62: 
L63: In the shared repository model, collaborators have push access to a single shared repository and create topic branches when they need to make changes. Pull requests are useful in this model because they start code review and general discussion about a set of changes before the changes are merged into the main development branch. This model is more common with small teams and organizations collaborating on private projects.

L11: # Best practices for using the REST API
L12: 
L13: Follow these best practices when using GitHub's API.
L14: 
L15: Copy as Markdown
L16: ## In this article
L17: 
L18:   * cite4†Avoid polling L19:   * cite5†Make authenticated requests L20:   * cite6†Avoid concurrent requests L21:   * cite7†Pause between mutative requests L22:   * cite8†Handle rate limit errors appropriately L23:   * cite9†Follow redirects L24:   * cite10†Do not manually parse URLs L25:   * cite11†Use conditional requests L26:   * cite12†Make requests that can be cached L27:   * cite13†Do not ignore errors L28:   * cite14†Further reading L29: ## cite4†Avoid polling L30: 
L31: You should subscribe to webhook events instead of polling the API for data. This will help your integration stay within the API rate limit. For more information, see cite15†Webhooks documentation .
L32: 
L33: If you cannot use webhooks and you must poll the API, poll as efficiently as possible to avoid exceeding the rate limit:
L34:   * Poll only as often as you need to, on a fixed schedule. If a response includes an `x-poll-interval` header, wait at least that many seconds before you poll the same endpoint again.
L35:   * Make authenticated conditional requests, so that unchanged data does not count against your primary rate limit. For more information, see cite11†Use conditional requests .
L36:   * Request only the data that you need, and keep responses stable, so that more of your polls return `304 Not Modified`. For more information, see cite12†Make requests that can be cached .
L37: ## cite5†Make authenticated requests L38: 
L39: Authenticated requests have a higher primary rate limit than unauthenticated requests. To avoid exceeding the rate limit, you should make authenticated requests. For more information, see cite16†Rate limits for the REST API .
L40: 
L41: ## cite6†Avoid concurrent requests L42: 
L43: To avoid exceeding secondary rate limits, you should make requests serially instead of concurrently. To achieve this, you can implement a queue system for requests.
L44: ## cite7†Pause between mutative requests L45: 
L46: If you are making a large number of `POST`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, or `DELETE` requests, wait at least one second between each request. This will help you avoid secondary rate limits.
L47: ## cite8†Handle rate limit errors appropriately L48: 
L49: If you receive a rate limit error, you should stop making requests temporarily according to these guidelines:
L50:   * If the `retry-after` response header is present, you should not retry your request until after that many seconds has elapsed.
L51:   * If the `x-ratelimit-remaining` header is `0`, you should not make another request until after the time specified by the `x-ratelimit-reset` header. The `x-ratelimit-reset` header is in UTC epoch seconds.
L52:   * Otherwise, wait for at least one minute before retrying. If your request continues to fail due to a secondary rate limit, wait for an exponentially increasing amount of time between retries, and throw an error after a specific number of retries.
L53: Continuing to make requests while you are rate limited may result in the banning of your integration.
L54: ## cite9†Follow redirects L55: 
L56: The GitHub REST API uses HTTP redirection where appropriate. You should assume that any request may result in a redirection. Receiving an HTTP redirection is not an error, and you should follow the redirect.
L57: 
L58: A `301` status code indicates permanent redirection. You should repeat your request to the URL specified by the `location` header. Additionally, you should update your code to use this URL for future requests.
L59: A `302` or `307` status code indicates temporary redirection. You should repeat your request to the URL specified by the `location` header. However, you should not update your code to use this URL for future requests.
L60: 
L61: Other redirection status codes may be used in accordance with HTTP specifications.
L62: ## cite10†Do not manually parse URLs L63: Many API endpoints return URL values for fields in the response body. You should not try to parse these URLs or to predict the structure of future URLs. This can cause your integration to break if GitHub changes the structure of the URL in the future. Instead, you should look for a field that contains the information that you need.
L64: For example, the endpoint to create an issue returns an `html_url` field with a value like `https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World/issues/1347` and a `number` field with a value like `1347`. If you need to know the number of the issue, use the `number` field instead of parsing the `html_url` field.
L65: Similarly, you should not try to manually construct pagination queries. Instead, you should use the link headers to determine what pages of results you can request. For more information, see cite17†Using pagination in the REST API .
L66: ## cite11†Use conditional requests L67: Most endpoints return an `etag` header, and many endpoints return a `last-modified` header. You can use the values of these headers to make conditional `GET` requests. If the response has not changed, you will receive a `304 Not Modified` response. Making a conditional request does not count against your primary rate limit if a `304` response is returned and the request was made while correctly authorized with an `Authorization` header.
L68: This makes conditional requests especially useful when you poll an endpoint, because each `304 Not Modified` response is fast and does not use your rate limit.
L69: In the following examples, replace `REDACTED` with your access token.
L70: 
L71: To make a conditional request with an `etag`:
L72: 
L73:   1. Make a request and save the value of the `etag` header from the response.
L74: 
L75:     `curl --include --header "Authorization: Bearer REDACTED" https://api.github.com/repos/octocat/Spoon-Knife/pulls
L76:     `
L77: 
L78: The response includes an `etag` header:

     3	The reviewed origin revision is `a162fb909d45b8bcdb54f1939f2230f0419423c1`.

     5	CI workflows, dependency configuration, and the service/deployment contracts.

    10	The main problem was failure handling: a green baseline did not prove that a
    11	reaction had been created, that an unreadable error was permanent, or that a
    12	validated job could form its promised URL. The existing package and Worker
    13	interfaces are small and useful. Broad restructuring would add churn without

    15	
    16	## Implemented findings
    17	
    18	### P2: Redirects could acknowledge a reaction that never happened
    19	
    20	At origin, `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor/src/github/reactions.ts`
    21	used default Fetch redirect handling and accepted any final `200` or `201`.
    22	A Workerd reproduction showed a `301` transforming the reaction POST into a
    23	GET with no body; a `200` reaction-list response then looked like successful
    24	creation. This matters when a repository URL redirects after a rename or move.
    25	
    26	The processor now repeats the original POST for `301`, `302`, `307`, and `308`,
    27	up to three redirects, only within `https://api.github.com` and without URL
    28	credentials. It retains the same token and body. Intermediate body cancellation
    29	does not delay the request. Unsafe, unsupported, or exhausted redirects follow
    30	the existing permanent-failure path. A real Worker integration fixture requires
    31	the redirected request to retain the exact method, credentials, and body.
    32	
    33	This follows GitHub's instruction to [repeat redirected requests](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#follow-redirects),
    34	accounts for [Fetch's POST-to-GET behavior](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-redirect-fetch),
    35	and avoids Cloudflare's [cross-host forwarding of authorization headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/request/#properties).
    36	
    37	### P2: Incomplete `403` diagnostics could discard retryable jobs
    38	
    39	The processor used error-body text to recognize secondary rate limits. It retried
    40	a timed-out `403` read, but acknowledged an errored or oversized read even though
    41	both also prevented classification. Existing tests explicitly expected that loss.
    42	
    43	Stream exceptions and the 16 KiB cutoff now produce `bodyReadFailed: true` and
    44	retry `403` responses. Header diagnostics and retry hints survive. Fully received
    45	empty or malformed bodies keep the status/header policy; other statuses keep
    46	their existing behavior. The one-second diagnostic deadline and best-effort
    47	cancellation remain intact. This policy applies GitHub's [rate-limit guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#handle-rate-limit-errors-appropriately)
    48	without treating a failed diagnostic read as proof of permanent denial.
    49	
    50	### P2: The broker client rejected valid OAuth response variants

    52	`packages/token-exchange/src/index.ts` required exactly `Bearer` and an explicit
    53	response `scope`. OAuth token types are case-insensitive, and an unchanged scope
    54	may be omitted. Valid responses therefore threw and caused unnecessary retries.
    55	
    56	The client accepts case variations of `Bearer` and uses the validated requested
    57	scope only when response scope is absent. Explicit scope values remain authoritative;

    59	still requires its existing expiration and issued-token-type fields. Literal
    60	response regressions failed four times before the fix and pass afterward.
    61	See [RFC 8693 §2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1)

    64	### P2: Accepted jobs could fail or change meaning during URL construction

    68	rejects. Signed deliveries could publish jobs that did not preserve the intended
    69	repository resource or failed before reaching the broker.
    70

    72	Tests preserve ordinary dotted names, percent literals, and well-formed Unicode.
    73	This is a canonical-resource correctness fix, not a demonstrated authentication
    74	bypass: queue writers and signed webhook bodies remain within the documented trust
    75	model. See the [URL dot-segment rules](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#single-dot-url-path-segment)
    76	and [ECMAScript URI encoding](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/global-object.html#sec-encodeuricomponent-uricomponent).
    77	
    78	### P3: Invalid UTF-8 was silently repaired before JSON parsing

    82	valid-JSON contract. Fatal UTF-8 decoding now shares the authenticated JSON error
    83	path and returns `400`. Bad signatures still return `401` before decoding.

    85	See [RFC 8259 §8.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-8.1)

    98	Ten version-specific cooldown exceptions had expired on 10 September. An isolated

   114	  including the adversarial non-enumerable-property case.

    25	## Webhook Worker flow

    27	`workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver/src/worker.ts` exposes only `POST /github/webhooks`. It rejects unknown routes and other methods before calling `handleGitHubWebhookRequest`.

1	# Adversarial implementation review — 12 September 2026
     2	
     3	The reviewed origin revision is `a162fb909d45b8bcdb54f1939f2230f0419423c1`.
     4	The review covered all three Workers, shared packages, unit and integration tests,
     5	CI workflows, dependency configuration, and the service/deployment contracts.
     6	Three collaborators independently examined ingress, processing/token exchange,
     7	and tooling; the implementation was then checked against the combined findings.
     8	The original checkout and its untracked research files were preserved in place.
     9	
    10	The main problem was failure handling: a green baseline did not prove that a
    11	reaction had been created, that an unreadable error was permanent, or that a
    12	validated job could form its promised URL. The existing package and Worker
    13	interfaces are small and useful. Broad restructuring would add churn without
    14	resolving these defects.
    15	
    16	## Implemented findings
    17	
    18	### P2: Redirects could acknowledge a reaction that never happened
    19	
    20	At origin, `workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor/src/github/reactions.ts`
    21	used default Fetch redirect handling and accepted any final `200` or `201`.
    22	A Workerd reproduction showed a `301` transforming the reaction POST into a
    23	GET with no body; a `200` reaction-list response then looked like successful
    24	creation. This matters when a repository URL redirects after a rename or move.
    25	
    26	The processor now repeats the original POST for `301`, `302`, `307`, and `308`,
    27	up to three redirects, only within `https://api.github.com` and without URL
    28	credentials. It retains the same token and body. Intermediate body cancellation
    29	does not delay the request. Unsafe, unsupported, or exhausted redirects follow
    30	the existing permanent-failure path. A real Worker integration fixture requires
    31	the redirected request to retain the exact method, credentials, and body.
    32	
    33	This follows GitHub's instruction to [repeat redirected requests](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#follow-redirects),
    34	accounts for [Fetch's POST-to-GET behavior](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-redirect-fetch),
    35	and avoids Cloudflare's [cross-host forwarding of authorization headers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/request/#properties).
    36	
    37	### P2: Incomplete `403` diagnostics could discard retryable jobs
    38	
    39	The processor used error-body text to recognize secondary rate limits. It retried
    40	a timed-out `403` read, but acknowledged an errored or oversized read even though
    41	both also prevented classification. Existing tests explicitly expected that loss.
    42	
    43	Stream exceptions and the 16 KiB cutoff now produce `bodyReadFailed: true` and
    44	retry `403` responses. Header diagnostics and retry hints survive. Fully received
    45	empty or malformed bodies keep the status/header policy; other statuses keep
    46	their existing behavior. The one-second diagnostic deadline and best-effort
    47	cancellation remain intact. This policy applies GitHub's [rate-limit guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api#handle-rate-limit-errors-appropriately)
    48	without treating a failed diagnostic read as proof of permanent denial.
    49	
    50	### P2: The broker client rejected valid OAuth response variants
    51	
    52	`packages/token-exchange/src/index.ts` required exactly `Bearer` and an explicit
    53	response `scope`. OAuth token types are case-insensitive, and an unchanged scope
    54	may be omitted. Valid responses therefore threw and caused unnecessary retries.
    55	
    56	The client accepts case variations of `Bearer` and uses the validated requested
    57	scope only when response scope is absent. Explicit scope values remain authoritative;
    58	null, empty, and non-string scopes remain invalid. The installation-token profile
    59	still requires its existing expiration and issued-token-type fields. Literal
    60	response regressions failed four times before the fix and pass afterward.
    61	See [RFC 8693 §2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1)
    62	and [RFC 6749 §5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749.html#section-5.1).
    63	
    64	### P2: Accepted jobs could fail or change meaning during URL construction
    65	
    66	`packages/github-webhook-jobs/src/index.ts` accepted `.` and `..` repository parts,
    67	which URL parsing normalizes, and lone surrogates, which `encodeURIComponent`
    68	rejects. Signed deliveries could publish jobs that did not preserve the intended
    69	repository resource or failed before reaching the broker.
    70	
    71	The shared parser now rejects these values before publication and consumption.
    72	Tests preserve ordinary dotted names, percent literals, and well-formed Unicode.
    73	This is a canonical-resource correctness fix, not a demonstrated authentication
    74	bypass: queue writers and signed webhook bodies remain within the documented trust
    75	model. See the [URL dot-segment rules](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#single-dot-url-path-segment)
    76	and [ECMAScript URI encoding](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/global-object.html#sec-encodeuricomponent-uricomponent).
    77	
    78	### P3: Invalid UTF-8 was silently repaired before JSON parsing
    79	
    80	The receiver authenticated exact bytes but decoded them with replacement before
    81	parsing JSON. Signed malformed UTF-8 could therefore receive `202` despite the
    82	valid-JSON contract. Fatal UTF-8 decoding now shares the authenticated JSON error
    83	path and returns `400`. Bad signatures still return `401` before decoding.
    84	Tests cover invalid bytes, overlong/truncated encodings, and valid non-ASCII text.
    85	See [RFC 8259 §8.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-8.1)
    86	and [TextDecoder error handling](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-textdecoder).
    87	
    88	### P3: Secret retrieval failures escaped the receiver's response contract
    89	
    90	A rejecting Secrets Store `get()` escaped the receiver handler instead of producing
    91	its documented configuration error. The receiver now returns `500` problem details
    92	with a fixed diagnostic event, excluding the exception's text, and publishes no
    93	job. The regression includes a secret-like failure message and checks the exact safe
    94	log. The asynchronous binding is described in [Cloudflare's Secrets Store integration](https://developers.cloudflare.com/secrets-store/integrations/workers/#3-access-the-secret-on-the-env-object).
    95	
    96	### P3: Expired dependency exceptions and contradictory README text
    97	
    98	Ten version-specific cooldown exceptions had expired on 10 September. An isolated
    99	archive without them passed `pnpm up -r --lockfile-only --ignore-scripts`,
   100	`pnpm dedupe --lockfile-only --ignore-scripts`, and
   101	`pnpm install --lockfile-only --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`. These were
   102	lockfile-only probes. The exceptions
   103	were removed; dependency versions and the source lockfile were preserved.
   104	See [pnpm's release-age exclusions](https://pnpm.io/10.x/settings#minimumreleaseageexclude).
   105	
   106	The README incorrectly said that all non-ping events created no job. It now states
   107	that newly created status comments create jobs. The service and implementation
   108	documents describe each changed behavior.
   109	
   110	## Simplification decisions
   111	
   112	- Exact job-key validation now checks the enumerable key set directly, removing
   113	  two sorts and a copied array. It retains the rejection of unexpected fields,
   114	  including the adversarial non-enumerable-property case.
   115	- The redirect policy stays private to reaction creation. A generic HTTP client,
   116	  configurable retry framework, or extra dependency interface would increase the
   117	  public surface for one operation.
   118	- The HTTP, job-contract, and token-exchange packages retain their existing
   119	  interfaces. Flattening them would spread shared validation or broker knowledge
   120	  across Workers and tests.
   121	- The queue and GitHub's existing-reaction success semantics already address
   122	  repeated delivery. An additional deduplication database is not justified by
   123	  the current operation.
   124	- Repository/author authorization, the permission pair, separate deployment
   125	  ownership, and separate CI workflows are explicit project choices. No evidence
   126	  justified silently replacing them during this review.
   127	
   128	## Remaining concerns and verification limits
   129	
   130	The source deployment-dispatch workflow does not pass the successful source SHA;
   131	the deployment updater follows the latest source branch. A successful revision A
   132	can therefore trigger a proposal containing newer revision B. At deployment commit
   133	`ebfec79b6abff60591578c8eea2a74349f56fefc`, the
   134	[updater follows the remote submodule branch](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot-deploy/blob/ebfec79b6abff60591578c8eea2a74349f56fefc/.github/workflows/update-cyspbot/update-submodule.sh#L6),
   135	and [downstream CI separately checks proposed source](https://github.com/chikachow/cyspbot-deploy/blob/ebfec79b6abff60591578c8eea2a74349f56fefc/.github/workflows/ci-source.yml#L29).
   136	This race is not evidence of an unchecked-deployment bypass; branch-rule enforcement
   137	was not inspected. Exact revision propagation needs a coordinated change in both
   138	repositories; only this project's implementation was changed here.
   139	
   140	Issuer RPC, broker response reading, and the initial GitHub fetch have no explicit
   141	application deadline. The existing byte limits do not bound elapsed time. This is
   142	a remaining resilience design question: choose budgets from dependency latency and
   143	queue-processing requirements, then test cancellation and error classification
   144	together. No production latency or outage was measured in this review.
   145	
   146	Local fixtures validate the issuer/broker interfaces and actual Worker execution;
   147	they do not validate production broker policy, live GitHub App permissions,
   148	production routes, queue provisioning, or Secrets Store permissions. No production
   149	deployment or live GitHub mutation was performed.
   150	
   151	## Validation and final review
   152	
   153	Baseline: `node --run check` passed all gates and 153 tests at the pinned origin.
   154	New regressions were first demonstrated against the original implementation.
   155	The implementation is committed as `6c74ede3c762fd21e7d5f1ab4a5fb49b041fafa8`.
   156	
   157	- Node 24 and pinned pnpm 10.34.5: frozen install and complete `node --run check`
   158	  pass, including formatting, environment/runtime types, lint, production/test
   159	  TypeScript, Knip, all 195 tests in 15 files, and all three Wrangler deploy dry runs.
   160	- `node --run test:coverage` passes on the committed implementation: 99.69%
   161	  statements, 98.51% branches, 98.18% functions, and 100% lines. The built-Worker
   162	  integration suite remains outside coverage instrumentation.
   163	- `git diff --check` passes. A final origin refresh still resolves to the reviewed
   164	  base. The dependency lockfile has no changes.
   165	
    24	
    25	## Webhook Worker flow
    26	
    27	`workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-receiver/src/worker.ts` exposes only `POST /github/webhooks`. It rejects unknown routes and other methods before calling `handleGitHubWebhookRequest`.
    28	
    29	`handleGitHubWebhookRequest` owns the HTTP response and privately authenticates the envelope. It:
    30	
    31	1. resolves `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` from a direct Worker secret or Secrets Store binding, mapping missing or unreadable secrets to a safe `500` problem response;
    32	2. requires `application/json` and reads at most `256 KiB`;
    33	3. requires the event, delivery, signature, and installation-target headers;
    34	4. requires the target type `integration` and the configured `GITHUB_APP_ID`;
    35	5. verifies the exact bytes and decoded signature with Web Crypto HMAC-SHA256 verification;
    36	6. decodes the authenticated body as UTF-8 with fatal error handling and parses it as JSON;
    37	7. classifies `issue_comment` deliveries with `action: "created"` and a trimmed comment body exactly equal to `/cyspbot status`;
    38	8. sends the derived version-1 job to `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_JOBS` and waits for the queue write; and
    39	9. returns the acknowledgement shape for ping, matching, or other events.
    40	
    41	The receiver resolves direct secrets and Secrets Store bindings through its private secret adapter.
    42	
    43	The receiver sends only a derived job to the queue. The job contains the kind, version, delivery ID, repository owner and name, and comment ID. The receiver uses the same job parser as the processor to validate the projected job before publication. It does not apply repository authorization filtering.
    44	
    45	## Webhook processor flow
    46	
    47	`workers/cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` consumes one message at a time from `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs`. It validates the versioned job, requests a GitHub App Installation Access Token with `issues:write pull_requests:write` for the canonical GitHub Repository Resource, and posts an `eyes` reaction to the comment. GitHub `200` and `201` responses complete the job. Its private redirect loop repeats the POST for supported redirects within `https://api.github.com`, with at most three redirects and no URL credentials; it cancels intermediate response bodies without awaiting cleanup.
    48	
    49	Cloudflare Queues delivers messages at least once. Repeated jobs are safe because the GitHub reaction operation treats an existing reaction as success. The consumer retries network failures, HTTP `429`, HTTP `5xx`, and rate-limited HTTP `403` responses. It acknowledges permanent failures, retries up to five times, and sends exhausted jobs to `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq`. GitHub HTTP error responses honor server waiting hints or use exponential backoff starting at 60 seconds, bounded to 24 hours; other transient failures use the queue's 60-second default.
    50	
    51	## Runtime bindings
    52	
    53	- `GITHUB_APP_ID`: required non-secret variable used to bind deliveries to the intended GitHub App.
    54	- `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: required Worker secret or Cloudflare Secrets Store binding.
    55	- `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_JOBS`: Queue producer binding used by the webhook receiver for derived status-reaction jobs.
    56	- `cyspbot-github-webhook-processor` consumes `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs` and sends exhausted jobs to `cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq`. GitHub HTTP error responses honor server waiting hints or use exponential backoff starting at 60 seconds, bounded to 24 hours; other transient failures use the queue's 60-second default.
    57	- The processor's `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_ISSUER`: RPC Service Binding to a separately deployed
    58	  `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` entrypoint. Its `issueToken(audience)` operation
    59	  returns an `IssuedToken`; the issuer deployment owns the workload subject
    60	  and signing details. This RPC is a workload-identity interface, not an OAuth
    61	  token endpoint.
    62	- The processor's `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN_AUDIENCE`: non-secret Worker variable containing the
    63	  logical audience requested from the issuer and accepted by the broker.
    64	- The processor's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER`: Service Binding used by the OAuth Client to call
    65	  the broker's existing RFC 8693 Token Endpoint with `fetch`.
    66	- The processor's `GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_BROKER_TOKEN_ENDPOINT`: non-secret Worker variable
    67	  containing the broker's token endpoint URL. It is separate from the logical
    68	  Workload Identity Token audience.
    69	
    70	The internal Token Exchange Client in `packages/token-exchange` first calls the issuer RPC, then posts the
    71	returned short-lived Workload Identity Token as a workload identity assertion
    72	to the configured broker endpoint as the RFC 8693 `subject_token` under the
    73	broker's OIDC ID Token subject-token profile. It requests a GitHub App
    74	Installation Access Token with a canonical GitHub `resource` and explicit permission
    75	`scope`; the broker remains the source of truth for normalization, OIDC ID
    76	Token profile verification, and Token Issuance Policy. On success, the client
    77	returns a `GitHubAppInstallationAccessToken`. Response validation accepts the
    78	case-insensitive `Bearer` token type and uses the requested scope when the broker
    79	omits an unchanged scope, preserving any explicit issued scope. On an OAuth failure, it throws a
    80	`GitHubAppTokenBrokerError` containing the HTTP status and OAuth error code and
    81	description. Workload identity assertions and issued GitHub tokens must not be
    82	logged.
    83	
    84	The client is an internal library operation and is not exposed as an HTTP
    85	route. Production service names, identity properties, domains, routes,
    86	resource identifiers, secret-store references, and Cloudflare Workload Identity
    87	properties belong to the separate deployment repository. The public Worker
    88	Wrangler files contain only local-development and dry-run service targets and
    89	values.
    90	
    91	## Tests and validation
    92	
    93	Tests live in each owning package or Worker’s `test/` directory alongside `src/`. Worker integration tests and their fixtures live under `test/integration/`; helpers shared by tests within a Worker live under its `test/support/`. The root `test/` contains the shared unit harness, its own test, and integration tests spanning multiple Workers. Tests use local source imports for internal seams and package imports for package interfaces and dependencies. Worker package exports expose only their entrypoints.
    94	
    95	The root `vitest.config.ts` selects the unit suite, three Worker integration suites, and the built-Worker integration suite, and owns combined coverage. Production TypeScript checks and the Node-import lint restriction apply to `src/`; the root test TypeScript configuration also covers package-local tests and their helpers. CI retains separate validation workflows.
    96	
    97	New commits cancel superseded CI runs for the same pull request. Every main push
    98	keeps its own CI run so successful checks can trigger the deployment update.
    99	The workspace's 72-hour minimum release age applies to local dependency resolution
   100	and the daily transitive updater, matching Dependabot's release-age floor.
   101	
   102	The unit and individual Worker integration suites run in Workerd through `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` with Vitest 4. Keep Vitest and its Istanbul coverage provider on matching versions supported by the published Cloudflare plugin. pnpm enforces peer dependencies, and Dependabot groups Cloudflare SDK and Vitest updates together. Vitest 5 updates are temporarily held in Dependabot until the published Cloudflare plugin supports them. Each Vitest project prohibits focused tests. Coverage explicitly includes package and Worker source files, including files not imported by tests, and excludes type declarations. Each Worker's production TypeScript check uses the runtime types generated from its Wrangler compatibility date and flags.
   103	
   104	The unit project exercises the root response, bounded body reading, request-body size and status handling, signature/target validation through HTTP responses, queue-job classification and processing, token-exchange response mapping, and all Worker factories. Separate Workerd integration projects load each Worker's real Wrangler configuration and entrypoint.
   105	
   106	The processor integration project loads the processor Wrangler configuration,
   107	runs a local `WorkloadIdentityIssuer` named-entrypoint fixture through a
   108	Workerd Service Binding, and exercises the queue entrypoint's token exchange.
    73	```
    74	
    75	The receiver waits for the queue write before returning `202`. Authenticated
    76	events that do not classify to this job receive `202` without a queue write.
    77	The receiver validates the derived job before publication: comment IDs must be positive safe integers, delivery IDs must be non-empty, and repository parts must be non-empty, at most 100 characters, and contain no path separators, query/fragment delimiters, or control characters. Repository parts must also be well-formed Unicode strings and cannot be `.` or `..`, so URL encoding neither throws nor changes the repository path. Payloads that cannot produce a valid job are acknowledged without a queue write. The receiver does not apply repository authorization filtering. A queue write failure
    78	returns `503 Service Unavailable`. GitHub does not automatically redeliver
    79	failed webhooks. Ingress is best effort until publication succeeds; operators
    80	manually redeliver failed deliveries after resolving the cause. See
    81	[delivery recovery](deployment.md#delivery-recovery).
    82	
    83	The processor requests a GitHub App Installation Access Token with
    84	`issues:write pull_requests:write` for the canonical GitHub Repository Resource and posts the
    85	`eyes` reaction to the comment. GitHub `200` and `201` responses complete the
    86	job. The processor follows at most three `301`, `302`, `307`, or `308` redirects,
    87	preserving the reaction POST, body, and authorization. Redirect destinations must
    88	remain on `https://api.github.com` without URL credentials. Other redirects,
    89	invalid destinations, and exhausted redirect chains are permanent failures.
    90	Cancellation of unused response bodies is best effort and does not
    91	delay acknowledgement or cause a retry. Network failures, `429`, `5xx`, and rate-limited `403` responses retry;
    92	other failures are acknowledged. The queue uses one-message batches, five
    93	retries, a 60-second default retry delay, and the
    94	`cyspbot-github-webhook-jobs-dlq` dead-letter queue. GitHub HTTP error responses honor numeric
    95	`Retry-After` and exhausted primary-quota `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers, using
    96	the longer wait with a 60-second minimum and Cloudflare's 24-hour maximum.
    97	Without a valid hint, GitHub HTTP error responses use exponential backoff starting at
    98	60 seconds, capped at 24 hours. Secondary-limit messages on `403` are
    99	retryable even when primary quota remains. Transport failures and other transient
   100	issuer or broker failures use the queue's 60-second default.
   101	
   102	GitHub error-body diagnostics have a one-second total read budget and a 16 KiB
   103	size limit. On timeout the processor cancels the unfinished read, retains status
   104	and header diagnostics, and logs `bodyReadTimedOut: true`. Stream failures and
   105	size-limit failures retain header diagnostics and log `bodyReadFailed: true`.
   106	These incomplete `403` bodies are retryable because their secondary-rate-limit
   107	classification is inconclusive. Fully received empty or malformed bodies retain
   108	the normal status/header policy.
   109	Other statuses retain their normal acknowledgement or retry policy.
   110	
   111	Rejections use RFC 9457-style problem-details JSON with `type`, `title`, and `status` fields:
   112	
   113	| Condition                                                  | Status |
   114	| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
   115	| Missing, empty, or unreadable webhook secret configuration |  `500` |
   116	| Non-JSON media type                                        |  `415` |
   117	| Body exceeds `256 KiB`                                     |  `413` |
   118	| Missing event, delivery, or signature header               |  `400` |
   119	| Target type or target App ID mismatch                      |  `401` |
   120	| Malformed or invalid signature                             |  `401` |
   121	| Authenticated body is not UTF-8 JSON                       |  `400` |
   122	| A matching job cannot be written to the queue              |  `503` |
   123	
   124	Repeated delivery IDs are accepted. Queue delivery is at least once, and the
   125	processor treats both successful GitHub reaction response statuses as
   126	completion, so repeated jobs do not require a separate deduplication store.
   127	
   128	## Token exchange responses
   129	
   130	The internal Token Exchange Client accepts the OAuth `Bearer` token type without
   131	regard to case. If the broker omits `scope`, the issued scope is the requested
   132	scope; an explicit scope must be a non-empty string and is returned as issued.
   133	The client still requires an access token, the access-token `issued_token_type`,
   134	and a positive integer `expires_in` for the broker's installation-token profile.
   135	These response rules follow [RFC 8693 section 2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html#section-2.2.1).
   136	
   137	## Logging and retention
   138	
   139	Rejected deliveries may log the delivery ID, event, Cloudflare Ray ID, and response status. Raw request bodies, signature values, and webhook secrets are not logged or retained.
   140	
   141	Processor failures log the queue message ID, delivery ID (at most 128 characters), attempt count, status, and bounded GitHub diagnostics or a recognized OAuth error code. Unrecognized broker codes are logged as `unrecognized_error`; broker descriptions and credentials are excluded.
